Exchange tokens

Equity-shaped, with the rights removed

A token issued by a trading venue, supported by that venue's profits, useful mainly on that venue. The closest thing crypto has to a share in a company — and a reminder of why shares come with legal rights.

The model

An exchange issues a token and gives it three jobs: discounts on trading fees for holders, priority access to new listings and launchpad sales, and a supply that shrinks as the exchange uses profits to buy back and burn tokens. The burn is the key mechanism: it ties the token's scarcity to the exchange's revenue in a way that looks a lot like a share buyback. Binance has burned roughly half of BNB's original supply this way, and BNB's chart tracks Binance's market share almost perfectly.

How it differs from equity

A shareholder owns a slice of the company: a claim on assets in bankruptcy, a vote, audited accounts, and legal recourse. A token holder has none of these. The burn is a policy the exchange can change (Crypto.com re-minted 70 billion previously burned CRO in 2025, with a vote dominated by the company's own holdings). Disclosure is whatever the exchange chooses. And the token's value is inseparable from the exchange's legal status: when the US sued Binance in 2023, BNB fell 25% in days, and when FTX collapsed, its FTT token — the collateral for much of the group's borrowing — went to zero in a week and took the exchange with it.

The FTT lesson

FTX's token was 'backed' by nothing but FTX, and FTX was backed in part by FTT. The exchange's affiliated trading firm held billions of FTT at inflated marks and borrowed customer deposits against it. When a rival exchange announced it would sell its FTT, the token's price collapsed, the loans went bad, and the hole in customer funds was exposed. The structure — a venue's own token as its own collateral — is the single most important thing to check about any exchange token, and it is not always visible from outside.

What to check

  • Is the exchange's revenue growing, and is the burn actually funded from it or from the treasury's own tokens?
  • What share of supply does the exchange still hold? Large holdings mean the 'market cap' is mostly a number.
  • Does the token have a life outside the exchange (BNB on BNB Chain, OKB on X Layer) or only inside it (LEO, KCS)?
  • Where is the exchange licensed, and what happened to the token the last time a regulator acted?
